analysis.one_liner: Replaces consumer bankruptcy with a simpler single chapter and lets people restructure mortgages, car loans, and student debt.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by one House Democrat with a single cosponsor twelve days before the 118th Congress ended and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tear up the current two-track consumer bankruptcy system and replace it with one simplified chapter. It would let people cut mortgage balances to what their homes are worth, pay off car loans at the car's actual value, erase student loan debt like any other debt, void forced-arbitration clauses, and close legal loopholes that let wealthy debtors shield assets. It was referred to two House committees and died there without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: People drowning in unaffordable debt. The bill would let them restructure home mortgages so foreclosure becomes avoidable, pay car loans based on the car's market value instead of the loan balance, discharge student loans on the same terms as other debt, and get through bankruptcy faster and cheaper, including through a streamlined 'limited proceeding' for simple cases [S2]. Its stated purpose includes reducing racial and gender disparities in bankruptcy outcomes and closing loopholes the wealthy use to avoid repaying creditors [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Creates a single Chapter 10 individual bankruptcy and repeals Chapter 13, replacing the current dual-track system with one process meant to be simpler and cheaper to navigate [S2].

Allows modification of mortgages on all residences and treatment of car loans based on the market value of the car, so borrowers can cure missed payments without late fees or penalty interest and avoid foreclosure or repossession [S2].
Makes student loan debt dischargeable on equal terms with most other debt, ending the special rule that has kept most private student loans unerasable [S2].
Voids pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers attached to property in the bankruptcy plan, and strengthens protections against illegal collection after discharge [S2].

Lets debtors with no ability to pay unsecured creditors get a discharge without filing any plan, reduces paperwork for routine cases, and lets debtors pay their attorneys through the plan instead of saving up before filing [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Secured lenders and creditors. Mortgage holders would no longer be able to block restructured home loans, auto lenders would take a hit when car loans are written down to market value, private student loan lenders would lose the protection that keeps their loans mostly unerasable, and debt collectors would face stronger enforcement of the discharge injunction [S2]. Some cost could be passed back to future borrowers through higher rates, which is the standard objection to letting courts rewrite loan terms.

drawbacks.text: Lenders argue that allowing courts to rewrite mortgage terms raises the cost of credit for everyone, because lenders price in the risk that loans can be cut down in bankruptcy; the bill's own findings dispute that restructurings raise financing costs [S2].

Creditors holding unsecured debt, like credit card and medical debt holders, would recover less in many cases, since the bill caps required payments based on a debtor's income above set thresholds and allows zero-payment discharges [S2].

The overhaul would force a massive transition: Chapter 13 is repealed outright, and judges, trustees, and the bar would have to rebuild practice around an entirely new chapter, with court rules rewritten under the bill [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households facing foreclosure, repossession, or unpayable student debt, the benefits are large and direct; the costs fall mostly on lenders, some of which would likely be passed into future loan pricing. The bill includes real safeguards for secured lenders, such as guaranteed payment values and default tolerances, but its design is aggressive and its complete lack of cosponsor momentum beyond one member suggests it had no realistic path even within the House.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-December 2024, referred to two House committees, and neither committee ever acted before the Congress expired in early January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Jerrold Nadler introduced the Consumer Bankruptcy Reform Act of 2024 in the House on December 18, 2024, joined by Representative Pramila Jayapal [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the House Financial Services Committee [S4].
It had one cosponsor, Representative Jayapal [S3].
No further action appears in the bill's history: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and servicers, auto lenders, private student loan lenders, and debt collectors keep the current rules that let them collect full loan balances and block discharge of most student debt. Debtors in financial distress get no relief.

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 18, 2024, proposing a complete replacement of the consumer bankruptcy system [S1].

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only member to do so [S3].

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (chaired by Rep. Jim Jordan)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during its roughly two weeks of life in the 118th Congress [S4].

against.name: House Financial Services Committee (chaired by Rep. Patrick McHenry)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill, which died without consideration before the Congress ended [S4].

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no partisan split is on the record; the only support shown was from two progressive House Democrats, and no Republican or other member signed on [S3].

industries.note: The bill would allow courts to restructure home mortgage loans on any residence and cure defaults without late fees or penalty interest, removing the lenders' current ability to block such changes. Their gain under the old rules comes from foreclosing on homes borrowers could otherwise save.

Car loans would be payable based on the vehicle's market value rather than the full loan balance, and repo rights would be curtailed for borrowers who stay reasonably current. Lenders currently collect more than the car is worth.

Student loans would become dischargeable like ordinary debt, ending the special protection that has kept most private student loans unerasable for life. The bill's findings state this protection never delivered lower borrowing costs.

The bill voids forced-arbitration and class-waiver clauses, strengthens the discharge injunction against post-bankruptcy collection, and creates penalties for predatory creditor behavior. Collectors currently profit from collection activity the fresh-start policy is supposed to bar.

The bill's stated purpose includes closing loopholes that let affluent, well-counseled debtors avoid repaying creditors while ordinary debtors face the full process. This is a direct hit on a practice available only to people who can afford expensive planning.

Simplified, court-funded procedures and attorney fees payable through plans could steady demand and reduce collection risk for consumer bankruptcy professionals, but a wholesale rewrite of Chapter 13 practice would disrupt an established bar and trustee system built around current law.
